Thursday afternoon through Friday: Active weather pattern is in 
store over the next 24-36 hours. There are a couple of areas worth 
monitoring on the synoptic scale that will bring both a period of 
wet weather and dry/windy weather conditions. The first area is 
associated with a deep closed low pressure system currently situated 
over the state of California. This low pressure system is draw 
northward a deep fetch of moisture off of the Gulf of 
California across the Southwest. There is a robust sub-tropical 
jet streak on the eastern flank of the low with speeds of up to 
around 95-100 kts at 250 mb. The sub-tropical jet will supply 
referencing moisture into the region and some dynamics aloft, 
but the bulk of the dynamics for our region will come via a cold
front being supplied by the Polar Jet and northern branch of 
the storm track.

The cold front will push across the Cascade Mountains after midnight 
tonight and strong frontogenesis will provide the forcing 
needed to squeeze out a good amount of moisture being advected 
in. The final part of the equation is the instability. Mid 
levels of the atmosphere will be moderately unstable with lapse 
rates of around 6.5 C/km. This will bring a convective element 
to the precipitation, especially this evening and then become 
less steep overnight as the regime transitions from showers to 
stratiform precipitation along the front. Clouds will increase 
this afternoon with an increasing chance for showers. A few of 
these showers may also include short- lived thunderstorms where 
there is a 10% chance over the Northeast Blue Mountains, L-C 
Valley, and Camas Prairie. Chances for rain increases to a near 
certainty by 8:00 to 10:00 PM generally along a line from 
Ritzville to Colville and points eastward. There's around a 70% 
chance of at least a quarter of an inch of rain and a 10-30% 
chance for spots receiving an inch or more of rain. This higher 
end of more than inch will more likely occur where we see bursts
of moderate to locally heavy rain under convectively enhanced 
cells.

Impacts with the rain will be mainly beneficial. There is potential 
for water to pond in low lying areas, especially for any areas where 
leaves and debris hasn't been cleared around drains. Seeing that 
much of the area is currently under a severe drought currently, this 
rain will be very beneficial.

Along with that northern branch of the storm track and cold front 
will be gusty north winds down the Okanogan Valley and a punch of 
much drier air. Water vapor satellite shows a lot of drying that is 
occurring in subsidence region on the backside of the advancing cold 
front. This punch of dry air will push across the Cascades and into 
eastern Washington early in the morning on Friday (after 4:00 AM). 
This will go along with strong cold air advection and a packing of 
the isobars with a northerly gradient across north-central WA. Gusty 
north winds with gust up to 40-50 mph is expected down the Okanogan 
Valley, across the Waterville Plateau, and into the western portion 
of the Columbia Basin. A Windy Advisory remains in effect
beginning a midnight and continues through 3:00 PM on Friday. 
Dew points will crash into the teens and potentially into the 
single digits along ridgetops for this portion of the forecast 
area as well. Winds will peak in the morning and then gradually 
decrease through the afternoon. There is a minor risk for fire 
spread in dry grasses and also for patchy blowing dust.

Friday night through Thursday: There is high confidence for 
temperatures to cool to right around normal with highs in the 50s. 
Low temperatures Friday night will be chilly cooling into the 20s 
across much of the region; the more sheltered northern valleys look 
to cool down into the lower 20s. Winds will be weakening overnight 
Friday and the dry air in place will promote strong radiational 
cooling at the surface. Doesn't look as cold heading through 
next week, but a lot of that will be dependent on the synoptic 
pattern and that still looks uncertain. About 60% of the model 
ensemble members supports an upper level low dropping south 
along the BC coast and ejecting across the region by late Sunday
into early next week. This leading scenario would bring 
precipitation to much of the region, but overall accumulations 
would be light. Then there is around 40% of the model ensembles 
that has the low further off to the west with ridging of higher 
pressure to more dominate the region. This slightly lower 
probability of possible outcomes would support a milder and dry 
forecast in the extended. /SVH
